section_summaries.epidemiology: Viral hepatitis occurs worldwide with varying epidemiology based on sanitary conditions and age. Hepatitis A is enterically transmitted, causing outbreaks often linked to contaminated water or food, with higher prevalence in low-income regions and risk to travelers. Hepatitis B is transmitted parenterally, sexually, and perinatally, with high prevalence in Asia and sub-Saharan Africa. Hepatitis C is mainly transmitted by injecting drug use in developed countries and through medical procedures in developing countries. Hepatitis D requires HBV for replication and is transmitted parenterally, sexually, and through household contacts. Hepatitis E is enterically transmitted, often water-borne, and a zoonosis, with rare cases in developed countries but significant outbreaks in endemic areas like the Indian subcontinent.
section_summaries.pathogenesis: Viral hepatitis involves viral replication in the liver, leading to hepatocellular damage often immunologically mediated. Chronic HBV and HCV are common causes of liver cirrhosis, influenced by infection duration, age, gender, alcohol consumption, and co-infections (HIV, HDV). HBV replication involves error-prone reverse transcription, predisposing to mutations affecting HBeAg production and leading to aggressive chronic hepatitis. HCV, an RNA virus, has high replication rates and lacks proofreading, generating numerous variants (quasi-species) that complicate immune responses. Chronic hepatitis C typically presents with lymphocytic inflammation and lymphoid aggregation in portal tracts, with potential microvesicular fatty changes, bile duct damage, and acidophilic changes in hepatocytes, eventually leading to cirrhosis.
section_summaries.clinical_manifestations: Acute viral hepatitis often presents with malaise, fatigue, anorexia, nausea, vomiting, jaundice, dark urine, abdominal pain, fever, and hepatomegaly, with elevated serum ALT, AST, and bilirubin levels. Symptoms usually abate within weeks, but fatigue can persist. Fulminant hepatitis, a rare severe complication with altered mental status and coagulopathy, is more common in HEV (especially in pregnant women) and HBV (with HDV co-infection), but rare in HAV and HCV. Chronic HBV and HCV infections can lead to cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) over decades, with symptoms like weight loss, right upper quadrant pain, and ascites. Chronic HBV carriers often have waxing and waning symptoms. HCV can also cause extrahepatic syndromes, including mixed cryoglobulinemia, glomerulonephritis, arthritis, type 2 diabetes, and non-Hodgkin's lymphoma. HDV co-infection is generally severe and potentially fulminant, while superinfection in chronic HBV patients often leads to more severe hepatitis and progression to cirrhosis. HEV clinical course is similar to HAV, and prolonged jaundice with fulminant hepatitis can occur, especially in pregnant women.
section_summaries.diagnosis: Diagnosis of viral hepatitis involves detecting virus-specific antibodies (IgM for acute infection, IgG for past or chronic infection) and/or viral antigens or nucleic acid (DNA/RNA for chronic infection and transmissibility). For HAV, IgM anti-HAV indicates acute infection. For HBV, HBV-DNA, HBsAg, HBeAg, anti-HBc (IgM/IgG), anti-HBe, and anti-HBs are used, with HBV-DNA correlating with viral replication and infectivity. For HDV, transient detection of HDAg or anti-HD indicates co-infection, and persistent anti-HD or HDV RNA/HDAg signifies chronic superinfection. For HCV, anti-HCV antibodies indicate prior or current infection, and HCV RNA detection by RT-PCR quantitates the virus and confirms ongoing infection. For HEV, acute infection is diagnosed by elevated ALT with HEV IgM or HEV RNA, or IgG seroconversion; chronic infection by persistent HEV RNA. Liver biopsy, ultrasonography, and non-invasive tests evaluate fibrosis and liver damage in chronic cases.
section_summaries.treatment: No specific antiviral treatment exists for acute HAV or HEV hepatitis; supportive care (rest, symptomatic management, silymarin) is important. For chronic HBV, various nucleos(t)ide analogs (lamivudine, tenofovir, adefovir, entecavir) and interferon formulations (PEG-interferon alpha-2a/2b) are used to suppress viral replication, prevent cirrhosis and HCC, and reduce mortality. Treatment decisions depend on HBV replication status, liver disease stage, and patient characteristics, aiming for viral suppression, ALT normalization, and HBeAg/HBsAg loss. For HDV, there is no specific antiviral treatment. For chronic HCV, treatment has significantly advanced with highly effective direct-acting antiviral (DAA) oral regimens, offering high cure rates (SVR) with fewer side effects, replacing older interferon-based therapies. DAAs are used for confirmed chronic infection, and pre- or post-exposure prophylaxis is not recommended.
section_summaries.prevention: Prevention of viral hepatitis involves improving sanitation, hygiene, and behavior modification. Effective vaccines are available for preventing HAV and HBV infections. HAV immunization involves passive immunoprophylaxis and inactivated vaccines, recommended for travelers and children. HBV vaccination is crucial, involving recombinant HBsAg vaccines administered in doses, and provides high protection for infants, children, and adults, along with post-exposure prophylaxis using HBIG and vaccine. HDV infection is prevented by HBV immunization. For HCV, prevention focuses on screening blood products, infection control practices (e.g., in healthcare settings), and reducing high-risk behaviors (e.g., injecting drug use), but there is no licensed vaccine due to viral heterogeneity. For HEV, control is primarily through improved hygiene, uncontaminated food/water, and recombinant HEV vaccines have shown efficacy but are not commercially available.
